name: remote-facade
intent: Provide a single coarse-grained facade over a web of fine-grained objects so that a remote client can complete a unit of work in one round trip, while the fine-grained objects keep their local-only interfaces and the facade stays free of domain logic.
problem: An object model tuned for in-process use has small objects with small methods and heavy interaction. Across a process boundary every one of those interactions becomes a marshalling, security and routing event, so one user action turns into dozens of remote calls; the decision is whether, and at which seam, to replace that chatty protocol with a few coarse operations.
context: Applies at any distribution boundary - a network hop, a service-mesh sidecar or merely a second process on the same host - where a fine-grained object model or service layer must be made remotely usable. It matters most when the interaction pattern is chatty (many small reads and writes per use case), when the model must not be exposed to remote clients, and when the transport is expensive relative to the work being done.
benefits: One round trip replaces many: collapsing a chatty protocol into a few coarse operations removes per-call latency, marshalling, security checks and packet overhead.
The fine-grained model stays local - no domain object grows a remote interface, so the model keeps its intention-revealing design and its freedom to change internally.
The remote surface is a single, explicit seam for authentication, authorisation, auditing, versioning and compatibility policy.
What crosses the wire is decoupled from the internal object graph: clients depend on named operations and payloads, not on the model's structure.
Coarse operations are a natural unit for caching, idempotency and retry policy, because each one corresponds to a use case rather than to a field access.
Client code becomes smaller and easier to test: the remote proxy is a narrow interface that can be substituted in tests.
tradeoffs: It is an extra layer with real cost: facade methods, transfer objects and the assembler between them must be written and maintained, and they drift from the model as the model evolves.

A coarse API suits clients unevenly - one client's whole use case in a single call is another client's over-fetching; batch granularity is a compromise, and blanket DTO use is explicitly not worth its mapping cost when the boundary is not remote.
A coarse call is not automatically an atomic one: transaction demarcation, partial-failure reporting and idempotency have to be designed for operations that touch several fine-grained objects.
Long-running coarse operations hold remote resources (connections, threads, database sessions) unless timeouts, deadlines and cancellation are part of the contract.
Contract coupling replaces object coupling: every client is bound to the facade's version, so the remote surface needs deliberate versioning and a deprecation story.
It hides the network, not the difficulty - orchestration, retries, concurrency conflicts and ordering remain the caller's problem.

participants.responsibility: Coarse-grained, stateless service object with a remote interface; its methods delegate to fine-grained objects, translate request and response data, and carry no domain logic of their own.
Hold the actual behaviour and state; they expose local interfaces only and are unaware that a remote caller exists.
Bundles the data of one coarse call into a serialisable payload so that remote method signatures never expose the object graph.
Generated or hand-written local stand-in that marshals the arguments, performs the transport call and unmarshals the result, making the facade look like a local object.
Converts between DTOs and domain objects at the boundary, keeping the mapping in one place instead of scattering it through the model.

use_cases: Enterprise application whose rich domain model is consumed by a thick client, another service or a batch job: the service layer gets a coarse remote interface instead of exposing entities and value objects.
Microservice boundary where a use case (place an order, update a shipment) must be a single call while the fine-grained aggregates stay internal to the service.
Legacy integration: a coarse adapter facade over an old object model so that new clients never see the legacy structure and the old model can be refactored behind it.
Mobile or high-latency clients, where every avoided round trip directly improves perceived latency and battery cost.
Batch and offline clients that need bulk operations (fetch a set, submit a set) instead of per-item calls.
Security boundary: one authenticated, authorised and audited entry point in front of the model.

Salesforce Composite API and Composite Graph API: a client submits related record operations, reference IDs and explicit all-or-none/graph boundaries in one request instead of making a remote call per sObject.
Microsoft Graph JSON batching: a `$batch` request groups up to 20 Graph operations behind one HTTP boundary while dependencies and per-request failures remain visible to the caller.
gRPC services such as the official RouteGuide example: generated stubs expose typed unary or streaming RPCs as the remote contract while the server's fine-grained implementation stays local.
avoid_when: The code already runs in a single address space - use a plain local Facade or a Module; a remote facade locally is pure overhead, and transfer objects there are harmful rather than useful.
The client and the model are both yours and the boundary has not been measured: do not introduce a distribution boundary speculatively just in case it is needed later.
A framework already exposes a coarse-grained HTTP/RPC API and the object model never leaves the process - a second facade on top is duplication.
The interaction is genuinely fine-grained and stateful (field-by-field editing): batching into coarse operations fights the protocol; prefer a session-oriented or replica-based design.
anti_patterns: Distributed objects: giving every fine-grained model object a remote interface so that one use case becomes N remote calls - exactly the problem a remote facade exists to fix.
God facade: every client request adds another method until the facade is a second, undocumented domain model that must be versioned in lockstep with each caller.
Entity leakage: returning live domain objects or lazy-loading proxies from remote methods, dragging persistence semantics and the object graph onto the wire.
DTO everywhere: applying transfer objects inside a single process, where the coarse-grained API is harder to use and the mapping work buys nothing.
Chatty facade: a 'coarse' facade whose methods still take one field at a time, renaming the problem instead of removing round trips.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: boundary mechanics (marshalling, policy, coarse orchestration) are separated from domain behaviour.
Information hiding: fine-grained objects are not exposed remotely; only the facade's operations and payloads are.
Single responsibility: the facade translates and delegates, while the domain model decides and holds the behaviour.
Dependency inversion: clients depend on the remote interface and the transfer objects, not on what lies behind the boundary.
Interface design by use case: one intention-revealing remote operation per unit of work.
best_practices: Design the remote interface from the client's use cases: name operations after them and size them so that a use case is one round trip.
Keep the facade stateless and free of domain logic; delegate to the service layer or domain model and put mapping in one assembler.
Send transfer objects, never live entities, and keep those objects transport-friendly (flat, serialisable, versionable).
Define the failure contract explicitly: deadlines, idempotency and retry rules, and how partial failure is reported to the caller.
Version the remote surface deliberately - add operations and fields compatibly instead of changing existing ones.
Measure before adding the boundary: introduce a remote facade only when round trips are demonstrably the cost, and keep the fine-grained model testable locally.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2003) - Remote Facade (chapter 15, Distribution Strategies).
